markdown:
Computer networking connects computers so they can exchange data. The Internet is built on a layered protocol stack. Each layer handles one responsibility: transport moves data between applications, the network layer routes packets between hosts, and the link layer delivers frames over a physical medium.

TCP, the Transmission Control Protocol, is a connection-oriented protocol that guarantees ordered delivery through acknowledgments and retransmission. A three-way handshake opens the connection: SYN, SYN-ACK, then ACK. Every byte is numbered, and unacknowledged segments are retransmitted after a timeout. This makes TCP reliable even over lossy networks.

UDP is a connectionless transport protocol with no handshake and no delivery guarantee. It suits low-latency uses such as live video streaming and voice over IP. Applications built on UDP must tolerate packet loss or recover from it themselves.

IP, the Internet Protocol, addresses and routes packets between hosts. Routers forward each packet hop by hop using routing tables. IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses, while IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses to solve address exhaustion. IP is unreliable by design; TCP repairs it when reliability is needed.

DNS, the Domain Name System, translates names like example.com into IP addresses. A resolver asks the root servers, which delegate to top-level domain servers, which delegate to authoritative name servers. Answers are cached with a time-to-live so repeated lookups are fast.

Routing protocols decide the path packets take. Distance-vector protocols like RIP share tables with neighbors and converge slowly. Link-state protocols like OSPF give every router a full topology map and run Dijkstra's algorithm. BGP connects the autonomous systems of the Internet.

A database system stores and manages structured data with integrity and controlled concurrent access. The relational model keeps data in tables of rows and columns, each row identified by a primary key. SQL is the standard interface for querying and modifying that data.

An index is a data structure that finds rows without scanning the whole table. A B-tree index keeps keys sorted in a balanced tree, so lookups take logarithmic time. Indexes on queried columns turn full table scans into direct lookups, at the cost of slower writes and extra storage.

Transactions bundle operations into an all-or-nothing unit of work. The ACID properties define correct behavior: atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability. Atomicity means every operation applies or none does. Durability promises that committed changes survive a crash, implemented with write-ahead logging.

Normalization structures tables to reduce redundancy and prevent update anomalies. Third normal form requires that no non-key column depends on another non-key column. Denormalization reintroduces redundancy on purpose to speed up reads in analytical workloads.

A query optimizer translates SQL into an execution plan. It chooses between index scans and full scans, and among join algorithms such as nested loops and hash joins. Cost estimates from table statistics guide the choice. The EXPLAIN statement reveals the chosen plan for tuning.

Concurrency control lets many transactions run safely at once. Multi-version concurrency control gives each transaction a consistent snapshot. Locking protocols trade throughput for strict isolation. Strong isolation can reduce parallelism, so engines offer configurable isolation levels.

An algorithm is a finite procedure that transforms input into output. Complexity analysis with Big-O notation describes how running time grows with input size. An O(n log n) algorithm scales far better than an O(n squared) one, though constant factors matter for small inputs.

Quicksort picks a pivot and partitions the array around it, recursing on both sides. It averages O(n log n) but degrades to quadratic on bad pivots. Merge sort splits, sorts, and merges halves for guaranteed O(n log n) at the cost of extra memory. Heapsort extracts maxima from a heap in place.

Graphs model relationships as vertices joined by edges. Breadth-first search explores level by level and finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs. Depth-first search dives deep before backtracking and supports cycle detection and topological sorting.

Dijkstra's algorithm computes shortest paths in weighted graphs with non-negative edges. It repeatedly extracts the closest frontier vertex. Bellman-Ford extends shortest paths to graphs with negative edge weights at a higher running cost.

Hash tables give expected constant-time lookup by hashing keys into array slots. Collisions are resolved with chaining or open addressing. When the load factor grows, the table is rehashed into a larger array to stay fast.

Dynamic programming solves problems with overlapping subproblems by storing each subproblem answer once. It needs optimal substructure. Classic cases are edit distance, knapsack, and longest common subsequence. Greedy algorithms make the locally best choice and suit problems like Huffman coding.
